An ornament sign is shorthand, and what it stands for has changed over 300 years. A small note
before a main note, or a **tr** over it, can mean four or five different things depending on when
and where the piece was written. Reading the sign isn't enough. **You have to know whose shorthand
it is.**

This page:

1. sets the five idioms side by side on one small note and one trill,
2. gives right and wrong readings for each period,
3. explains where improvisation fits, then and now,
4. ends with a [flow chart](#flowchart) that walks you from the ornament in front of you to a way
   to play it.

Press **▶** on any example to hear it. The notes shown are what is played, not just what is
written.

The key line runs between Classical and Romantic. **Before about 1820 the small note is a real
note that takes the beat and much of the main note's time. After that it's usually a quick flick,
and from the 20th century it goes before the beat.**

## Baroque: the player finishes the music {#baroque}

A Baroque score is incomplete on purpose. Composers expected the player to add graces, and in
France each composer printed a table of his own signs (d'Anglebert 1689, Couperin 1713). The
defaults are clear: **ornaments start on the beat, and from the note above** (J. S. Bach; C. P. E.
Bach). How many to add, and where, is taste. Some scholars argue that Bach's trills could start
on the main note too (Neumann, *Ornamentation in Baroque*). Most players today still start them
from above.

Here is the opening of the Sarabande from Bach's English Suite No. 3, as plain as Bach wrote it
the first time. He then wrote out an ornamented version of his own (*Les agréments de la même
Sarabande*).

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:20
T:Bach, Sarabande, English Suite No. 3 (BWV 808): the theme
M:3/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
BA A3 c/B/ | cA ^F3 A/G/ | AE E2 PD>C | B,3 A, G,2 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-ok">Valid</div>

**French style: graces on the strong notes.** An appoggiatura leans on beat 2, where a sarabande
puts its weight. A trill from above goes on the leading tone, and a mordent on the last note.
The tune stays the same.

```{=html}
<div class="ax-pair">
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:21
T:Written
M:3/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
B{B}A A3 c/B/ | cA T^F3 A/G/ | AE E2 D>C | B,3 A, MG,2 |]
</script><script type="text/plain" data-play>
X:22
M:3/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
B2 B2A2 A4 c B | c2A2 G^FG^F^F2 A G | A2E2 E4 D3C | B,6 A,2 G,=F, G,2 |]
</script></div>
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:22
T:Played
M:3/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
B2 B2A2 A4 c B | c2A2 G^FG^F^F2 A G | A2E2 E4 D3C | B,6 A,2 G,=F, G,2 |]
</script></div>
</div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-ok">Valid</div>

**Italian style: fill in the long notes.** The long notes become running notes (*passaggi*, or
divisions) that circle the written pitch. The notes on the beat are still Bach's, so the harmony
doesn't change.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:23
T:Divisions on the long notes
M:3/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
BA AG/A/ Bc/B/ | cA ^F/G/A/^F/ G A/G/ | AE E/^F/G/E/ D>C | B,3 A, G,2 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-no">Not appropriate</div>

**Ornaments everywhere, and a trill on the resolution.** A mordent on every note flattens the
dance: beat 2 no longer stands out. The trill on the final G is the worst of it. A trill adds
tension, so it belongs on the note *before* the resolution, never on the resolution itself.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:24
T:Too much, in the wrong places
M:3/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
MBMA MA3 Mc/MB/ | McMA M^F3 MA/MG/ | MAME ME2 MD>MC | MB,3 MA, TG,2 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-no">Not appropriate</div>

**A 19th-century reading.** The trill starts on the main note, and the grace on beat 2 is crushed
into a flick before the beat. Both are right in Chopin. Here they lose the two dissonances, the
leaning A against B♭ and the trill's upper note, that the Baroque ornaments exist to make.

```{=html}
<div class="ax-pair">
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">

T:Written
M:3/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
B{B}A A3 c/B/ | cA T^F3 A/G/ | AE E2 D>C | B,3 A, G,2 |]
</script><script type="text/plain" data-play>
X:26
M:3/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
B B A2 A6 c B | c2A2 ^FG^FG^F2 A G | A2E2 E4 D3C | B,6 A,2 G,4 |]
</script></div>
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:26
T:Played
M:3/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
```

## Classical: written down more, still on the beat {#classical}

The rules hardly change from the late Baroque. **Appoggiaturas fall on the beat and take half the
main note**, or two-thirds of a dotted one (Leopold Mozart; Türk; Clementi), and trills start
from the note above. What changes is how much the composer writes. Mozart often writes his
appoggiaturas as full-size notes and writes out the decorations of a slow movement, so there is
less for the player to add (Neumann, *Ornamentation and Improvisation in Mozart*). There are still
two places to improvise: the **cadenza** at the fermata in a concerto, and the short **Eingang**
(lead-in) at a pause before a theme comes back.

The phrase below is written for this page in the Classical style.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:30
T:Written
M:2/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=66
K:F
{d}c2 B A | {A}G2 F2 | A c {g}f e | Td3/2 c/ c2 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-ok">Valid</div>

**The textbook reading.** Each appoggiatura takes half its note, on the beat. The short grace
before the quick F is short, and the trill starts from above and ends on a quick anticipation of
the last note.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:31
T:Played
M:2/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=66
K:F
d2 c2 B2 A2 | A2 G2 F4 | A2 c2 g f e2 | e/d/e/d/e/d/ c c4 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-ok">Valid</div>

**On the repeat, a little more.** A turn fills the first bar and a rising figure leads into the
third. Every decoration starts and ends on the written notes. This is what Mozart writes out
himself when a melody comes back.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:32
T:Played, second time
M:2/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=66
K:F
d2 c2 BcBA | A2 G2 F2 E F G | A2 c2 g f e2 | e/d/e/d/e/d/ c c4 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-no">Not appropriate</div>

**Crushed graces and a main-note trill.** Every appoggiatura is flicked away, so the sighs
(D against C, A against G) disappear. Leopold Mozart and Türk both treat the long appoggiatura
as the expressive heart of the phrase. The trill from the main note is the 19th-century habit.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:33
T:Played
M:2/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=66
K:F
d/c7/2 B2 A2 | A/G7/2 F4 | A2 c2 g/f3/2 e2 | d/e/d/e/d/e/ c c4 |]
</script></div>
```

## Romantic: short, and the composer decides {#romantic}

Through the 19th century grace notes get shorter and move towards (or before) the beat, and
trills start on the main note (Brown; Hummel). Composers write ever more precisely what they
want, and the player's job shifts from **adding** ornaments to **shaping** the ones written.
Chopin is the famous exception: grace notes and trills **start with the bass note**, on the beat
(Eigeldinger; Ekier).

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:40
T:Written (in the style of a nocturne)
M:2/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=54
K:Eb
V:1
{c}B4 G2 F2 | TF4 E4 |]
V:2 clef=bass
E,,2 B,,2 G,2 B,,2 | B,,,2 A,,2 E,,4 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-ok">Valid (Chopin)</div>

**With the bass.** The grace note sounds together with the low E♭, as a quick lean, and the trill
starts on its main note F.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:41
T:Played
M:2/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=54
K:Eb
V:1
c B3 G2 F2 | F/G/F/G/F/G/E/F/ E4 |]
V:2 clef=bass
E,,2 B,,2 G,2 B,,2 | B,,,2 A,,2 E,,4 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-ok">Valid (later 19th century)</div>

**Before the beat.** In much later Romantic music (and in Chopin's early Contredanse, by his
editors' reading) the grace goes before the beat, so the bass and the main note sound together
(Brown; Ekier).

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:42
T:Played
M:2/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=54
K:Eb
V:1
z7 c | B4 G2 F2 | F/G/F/G/F/G/E/F/ E4 |]
V:2 clef=bass
z8 | E,,2 B,,2 G,2 B,,2 | B,,,2 A,,2 E,,4 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-no">Not appropriate</div>

**A Baroque appoggiatura.** A long lean on C takes half the beat and smothers the melody's first
note. The trill starts from above, and an extra turn is added. None of it was asked for: by now
the composer writes what he wants.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:43
T:Played
M:2/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=54
K:Eb
V:1
c2 B2 G2 F2 | GFEF E4 |]
V:2 clef=bass
E,,2 B,,2 G,2 B,,2 | B,,,2 A,,2 E,,4 |]
</script></div>
```

## 20th and 21st century: read the legend {#modern}

Concert music after about 1900 mostly writes out exactly what it wants. Where signs survive,
the general conventions are: **grace notes before the beat, trills from the main note and as fast
as possible**, and nothing added (Gould). Many scores invent their own signs, for microtones,
trills that speed up or slow down, or extended techniques, and explain them in a **performance
note** at the front. That note overrules any period rule. Improvisation returns in a new form:
some scores give a box of notes to repeat freely, or a graphic to interpret, and say so.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:50
T:Written
M:2/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=60
K:C
z4 {e}d4 | Tc4 B4 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-ok">Valid</div>

**The default.** The grace goes before the beat, and the trill is unmeasured from the main note.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:51
T:Played
M:2/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=60
K:C
z3 e d4 | c/d/c/d/c/d/c/d/ B4 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-ok">Valid, if the legend says so</div>

**On the beat.** Some composers ask for graces on the beat. If the performance note says so,
that's the right reading, and only then.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:52
T:Played
M:2/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=60
K:C
z4 e d3 | c/d/c/d/c/d/c/d/ B4 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-no">Not appropriate</div>

**A Baroque reading.** A long appoggiatura on the beat and a trill from above would be right in
Bach. Here they change the composer's rhythm and harmony.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:53
T:Played
M:2/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=60
K:C
z4 e2 d2 | dcdc B4 |]
</script></div>
```

## Jazz: the player owns the sound {#jazz}

In jazz the written notes are an outline. Grace notes, falls and scoops are part of a player's
**sound**: they come before or across the beat, in swing time, and are mostly not written at all
(Caniato). A big-band chart writes them as signs (fall, doit, scoop, plop, shake), and the
section plays them the way its **lead player** does. Singers and soloists add them freely.
▶ plays the slides on a clean electric guitar, so a fall really falls.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex" data-style="swing"><script type="text/plain">
X:60
T:Written (lead sheet)
M:4/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=120
K:C
"C7"G2 E G c4 |]
</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-ok">Valid</div>

**A fall off the long note.** The line is swung, and the last note falls away at its release,
never before the beat.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:61
T:With a fall
M:4/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=120
K:C
G2 E G "^fall"c4 |]
</script><script type="text/plain" data-bend>{"bpm": 120, "sound": "clguitar", "notes": [{"t": 0, "d": 1, "midi": 67}, {"t": 1, "d": 0.66, "midi": 64}, {"t": 1.66, "d": 0.34, "midi": 67}, {"t": 2, "d": 2, "midi": 72, "bend": [[0, 0], [1.2, 0], [2, -7]]}]}</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-ok">Valid</div>

**Scoop in, shake out.** The first note slides up from below, and the long note gets a shake
after it has sounded straight for a moment. That's Armstrong's "terminal vibrato" made wider
(Schuller).

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:62
T:Scoop and shake
M:4/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=120
K:C
"^scoop"G2 E G "^shake"c4 |]
</script><script type="text/plain" data-bend>{"bpm": 120, "sound": "clguitar", "notes": [{"t": 0, "d": 1, "midi": 67, "bend": [[0, -2], [0.25, 0]]}, {"t": 1, "d": 0.66, "midi": 64}, {"t": 1.66, "d": 0.34, "midi": 67}, {"t": 2, "d": 2, "midi": 72, "bend": [[0, 0], [0.5, 0], [0.6, 3], [0.7, 0], [0.8, 3], [0.9, 0], [1, 3], [1.1, 0], [1.2, 3], [1.3, 0], [1.4, 3], [1.5, 0], [1.6, 3], [1.7, 0]]}]}</script></div>
```

<div class="ob-verdict ob-no">Not appropriate</div>

**A Classical trill, played straight.** Even eighths and a measured trill from above, closed with
a neat turn. Every note is "right", but the line no longer swings, and a jazz shake is looser and
wider than this.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:63
T:Played
M:4/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=120
K:C
G4 E2 G2 dcdcdcBc |]
</script></div>
```

## Improvisation, then and now {#improvisation}

Ornaments are what remains in the notation of a much larger habit of making music up on the
spot. How much of that habit a score expects changes from period to period:

| Period | What the player was expected to invent | Today |
|---|---|---|
| Baroque | Graces on almost any note; divisions on slow movements, above all on the repeat; the chords over a figured bass; cadenzas at fermatas (C. P. E. Bach; Quantz) | Early-music players add their own again. Bach's written-out *agréments* and ornamented editions of Corelli's slow movements are the models. |
| Classical | Cadenzas in concertos, Eingänge at pauses, decoration of repeats in slow movements and arias (Neumann, *Ornamentation and Improvisation in Mozart*) | Players play written cadenzas (Mozart's own, Beethoven's) or write their own; singers decorate the repeats in Mozart's arias. |
| Romantic | Less and less: composers write the ornaments and the cadenzas themselves | Play what's written. Shape the written ornaments with rubato and tone instead of adding to them. |
| 20th and 21st century | Nothing, unless the score asks. Then sometimes a great deal: free repetition, graphic scores, open form. | Follow the performance note. |
| Jazz | Almost everything: the melody's shape, the ornaments, the solo | The heart of the style. The written melody is a starting point. |

Two things hold across all of them:

- **Ornaments serve the structure.** Baroque, Classical and jazz improvisers all decorate weak
  notes and long notes, and leave the arrivals (cadences, downbeats, chord tones) clear.
- **More isn't better.** C. P. E. Bach compared too many ornaments to too much seasoning
  (C. P. E. Bach, ch. 2). A Basie section player would say much the same about a fall on every
  note.

## Which way do I play it? {#flowchart}

## Works Cited
<!-- works-cited: written by scripts/works-cited.py -->
::: {.works-cited}
Anglebert, Jean-Henry d'. *Pièces de clavecin ... Livre premier*. Paris, 1689. IMSLP. [imslp.org/wiki/Pi%C3%A8ces_de_clavecin_(Anglebert,_Jean-Henri_d%27)](https://imslp.org/wiki/Pi%C3%A8ces_de_clavecin_(Anglebert,_Jean-Henri_d%27)). "Marques des Agrements et leur signification", read from the 1689 print (IMSLP #110970).

Bach, Carl Philipp Emanuel. *Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments*. Translated and edited by William J. Mitchell, W. W. Norton, 1949. First published as *Versuch über die wahre Art das Clavier zu spielen*, 1753. Ch. 2, Embellishments.

Bach, Johann Sebastian. *Clavier-Büchlein vor Wilhelm Friedemann Bach*. Manuscript, begun 22 Jan. 1720. Yale University, Irving S. Gilmore Music Library. [collections.library.yale.edu/catalog/10991080](https://collections.library.yale.edu/catalog/10991080). The *Explication unterschiedlicher Zeichen* is on leaf 3v (IIIF image 10991088); the table on this page is read from it.

Barnhart, Scotty. *The World of Jazz Trumpet: A Comprehensive History and Practical Philosophy*. Hal Leonard, 2005.

Brown, Clive. *Classical and Romantic Performing Practice 1750–1900*. Oxford UP, 1999.

Caniato, Michele. *The Jazz Ensemble Companion*. R&L Education, 2009. Table B.10, "Expressive devices".

Clementi, Muzio. *Introduction to the Art of Playing on the Piano Forte*. London, Clementi, Banger, Hyde, Collard & Davis, [1801]. Internet Archive. [archive.org/details/imslp-to-the-art-of-playing-the-pianoforte-op42-clementi-muzio](https://archive.org/details/imslp-to-the-art-of-playing-the-pianoforte-op42-clementi-muzio). Graces, pp. 10-11.

Couperin, François. *L'Art de toucher le clavecin*. Paris, 1716. Edited by Nicolas Sceaux, 2008. IMSLP. [imslp.org/wiki/L%27art_de_toucher_le_clavecin_(Couperin,_Fran%C3%A7ois)](https://imslp.org/wiki/L%27art_de_toucher_le_clavecin_(Couperin,_Fran%C3%A7ois)). "Agréments qui servent au jeu", pp. 6-7 (IMSLP #22200).

Eigeldinger, Jean-Jacques. *Chopin: Pianist and Teacher as Seen by His Pupils*. Edited by Roy Howat, translated by Naomi Shohet et al., Cambridge UP, 1986.

Ekier, Jan, editor. *Wydanie Narodowe Dzieł Fryderyka Chopina* (National Edition). Polskie Wydawnictwo Muzyczne. Performance commentaries. Commentary to Various Compositions (WN 27, WN 56); introduction, "Ozdobniki".

Gould, Elaine. *Behind Bars: The Definitive Guide to Music Notation*. Faber Music, 2011. Grace notes, trills and other ornaments in modern notation.

Hummel, Johann Nepomuk. *Ausführliche theoretisch-practische Anweisung zum Piano-Forte-Spiel*. Vienna, Tobias Haslinger, 1828. Internet Archive. [archive.org/details/ausfhrlichetheor00humm](https://archive.org/details/ausfhrlichetheor00humm). Part III, "Von den Verzierungen", pp. 393-402.

Mozart, Leopold. *A Treatise on the Fundamental Principles of Violin Playing*. Translated by Editha Knocker, Oxford UP, 1948. First published as *Versuch einer gründlichen Violinschule*, 1756.

Neumann, Frederick. *Ornamentation and Improvisation in Mozart*. Princeton UP, 1986.

Neumann, Frederick. *Ornamentation in Baroque and Post-Baroque Music, with Special Emphasis on J. S. Bach*. Princeton UP, 1978.

Pejrolo, Andrea, and Richard DeRosa. *Acoustic and MIDI Orchestration for the Contemporary Composer*. Focal Press, 2009. Falls, doits and the shake.

Purcell, Henry. *A Choice Collection of Lessons for the Harpsichord or Spinnet*. London, Frances Purcell, 1696. Internet Archive. [archive.org/details/bim_early-english-books-1641-1700_a-choice-collection-of-l_purcell-henry_1696](https://archive.org/details/bim_early-english-books-1641-1700_a-choice-collection-of-l_purcell-henry_1696). "Rules for Graces".

Quantz, Johann Joachim. *On Playing the Flute*. Translated by Edward R. Reilly, 2nd ed., Northeastern UP, 2001. First published as *Versuch einer Anweisung die Flöte traversiere zu spielen*, 1752.

Schuller, Gunther. *Early Jazz: Its Roots and Musical Development*. Oxford UP, 1968. The Armstrong chapter, on terminal vibrato and the shake.

Türk, Daniel Gottlob. *School of Clavier Playing*. Translated by Raymond H. Haggh, U of Nebraska P, 1982. First published as *Klavierschule*, 1789. Ch. 3 appoggiaturas, ch. 4 essential ornaments.
:::
